article.headline: Curated Lists Beat the Algorithm, Says Tech Veteran Scoble
article.lede: Robert Scoble, a blogger who built his reputation chronicling Silicon Valley for two decades, has a simple prescription for anyone frustrated by X's algorithmic feed: abandon it. His recommendation — curated lists consumed through X Pro — restates a debate as old as the social-media era itself: who should decide what you read, you or the platform?
article.body:
The **For You feed** is X's default experience: a ranked, algorithmically assembled stream that mixes posts from accounts you follow with content the system predicts you'll engage with. Engagement-optimised feeds tend to surface the provocative and the viral over the merely good, a dynamic that has made "doomscrolling" a clinical-sounding complaint rather than a metaphor.

*X Pro* — the paid, column-based dashboard formerly known as TweetDeck before Elon Musk's acquisition rebranded and paywalled it — offers a different model. Users build columns around lists: manually curated groups of accounts. Nothing enters a list column unless a human put that account there. The result is closer to a personalised newspaper masthead than a recommendation engine.

Scoble's implicit argument is that for *Tech Twitter* — the loose community of engineers, founders, and observers who have gathered on the platform since the mid-2000s — signal quality matters more than reach. A list of two hundred carefully chosen technologists, followed chronologically, will surface substantive thinking that an engagement-maximising algorithm is structurally incentivised to bury in favour of hot takes.

The broader tension Scoble is pointing at is genuine. Platform algorithms optimise for the metric their owners care about — time-on-site, ad impressions, subscription retention — which may or may not align with what an individual reader values. Curated lists hand that editorial judgment back to the user, at the cost of requiring the user to exercise it. The tradeoff is effort for quality: a reasonable trade for a professional audience, a harder sell for a casual one.

There is nothing technically novel here. Lists have existed on Twitter since 2009. What has changed is the default: as algorithmic feeds have grown more aggressive, the case for opting out has grown louder, and Scoble's terse endorsement is one data point in a longer argument many power users are having about reclaiming their own attention.

concepts.definition: X's default algorithmically ranked timeline. Rather than showing posts in chronological order from followed accounts, it uses engagement signals and predicted interest to surface content from both followed and unfollowed accounts. Critics argue it rewards provocation over substance.

A paid, column-based dashboard for X (formerly called TweetDeck). It lets users run multiple chronological streams side by side — by list, search term, or notification type — without algorithmic reranking. Access was placed behind a subscription after Twitter's acquisition and rebranding as X.

A feature allowing users to group any set of X accounts into a named collection. Posts from list members appear in a separate, chronological feed. Lists can be public or private and are unaffected by the platform's recommendation algorithm.

A content stream ranked by a platform's machine-learning model rather than by time. The model typically optimises for an engagement proxy — likes, replies, watch time — which can diverge from what users say they want when surveyed. Most major social platforms shifted to algorithmic defaults in the mid-2010s.

poster_scobleizer.blurb: Robert Scoble is a prominent tech blogger, author, and entrepreneur known for his early coverage of Microsoft and Silicon Valley. He posts about emerging technologies, including AI, augmented reality, and startups, and has over 200,000 followers on X.
poster_scobleizer.credibility_note: Scoble has faced criticism for overly optimistic tech predictions and was involved in a 2017 sexual misconduct allegation, which he denied.
